title: Video review
summary: A collection of nouns and verbs for reviewing a video with a fixed rubric, run by a person or a worker that did not make it: panels of the exact bytes at the sizes people watch on, every number traced to its evidence, timestamped findings with a severity, the evidence seen and the verb that would fix each one, a second opinion where reviewers disagree, a person who watches and listens, and a re-review of the fixed cut.
boundaries: A review is by a person or a worker that did not make the cut, and it names the exact bytes it watched.
A review recommends; only a person approves publishing, outside this pack.
Findings and reviews stay on the record; a re-review answers every earlier finding.
Workers create nouns and propose verbs; an authorized requester enqueues the proposals worth doing.
Importing the pack writes nothing and enqueues nothing.

nouns.title: A collection of nouns and verbs for reviewing a video with a fixed rubric, run by a person or a worker that did not make it

value.lets_workers: Review a video against a fixed ten-area rubric as a person or a worker that did not make it: panels of the exact bytes, sized for the screens people will watch on; every number traced to its evidence; timestamped findings with a severity, what was seen, how it was seen and the verb that would fix it; a second reviewer's comparison where reviewers disagree; a person who watches and listens; findings routed to the verbs that fix their causes; and a re-review of the fixed cut against the same finding ids.

Contact sheets, strips and display-scale sheets of those bytes.
Every number and claim, traced before the story is judged.
The rubric, findings, scores, top fixes and a decision.
A second reviewer on the same panels; disagreements get a second look.
A person watches start to finish and listens on headphones and a phone speaker.
Each finding to the verb that fixes its cause, grouped by cause.
The fixed cut, against every earlier finding id.
Only the owner releases or holds, and records which.

value.worked_example: Made-up: a 45-second explainer for a fictional pantry. The claim trace disputes one number, the review finds seven problems from a blocker to a note and decides revise, and the re-review of the fixed cut finds the blocker fixed, one minor not fixed and one new minor, and decides ready for the owner.
value.complements: The video showcase pack's review-video decides whether a cut is ready; this pack gives that decision a fixed rubric, timestamped findings, routes to fix verbs and a re-review. The video QA pack measures; this pack judges with the measurements in hand.
provenance_notes: Generalizes an adversarial review practice from a working short-form video studio: assume problems until the panels show otherwise, give a timestamp and what was seen for every claim, fixed question banks with scores, a second model on the same panels with disagreements looked at again, fixes routed to the template that caused them, and reviews bound to the exact master hash.

Applied to ta-amps's own 3:00 explainer film on October 30, 2026 while this pack was written: a review of its second final cut with 23 findings and a top-ten list, kept privately with the film's evidence.

nouns.title: Rubric: ten areas and the questions a reviewer answers
nouns.category_reason: A fixed question bank with pass criteria and the severity of each failure, the suite every review answers.

story_and_hook.question: What happens on screen in the first second, and would a viewer who did not choose this video keep watching?
story_and_hook.passes_when: Something visibly changes from the first frame, and the opening line, spoken and shown, opens a question the video answers.

story_and_hook.question: Does the opening promise only what the video delivers, with no invented record, deadline or contradiction?
story_and_hook.passes_when: Every promise in the first 3 s is paid off later in the cut.

story_and_hook.question: Is there a setup, a turn and a payoff, in that order, and does each act say why it follows the last?
story_and_hook.passes_when: A bridge line or picture joins every act.

clarity.question: With the sound off, is the point clear from the frames alone?
clarity.passes_when: The contact sheet, read without audio, tells the story.

clarity.question: Could a first-time viewer say in one sentence what it does and who it is for?
clarity.passes_when: The reviewer's own one-sentence summary matches the brief; real viewers are the video audience acceptance pack's work.

clarity.question: Is any word used on screen before it is explained?
clarity.passes_when: Every new term is spoken or shown with its meaning the first time.

pacing.question: Is there a new visual event at least every 3 s, outside declared holds?
pacing.passes_when: The cut cadence row has no stretch warnings, or each has a written reason.

pacing.question: Does any shot ask the viewer to read a paragraph while the voice says something else?
pacing.passes_when: On-screen words either repeat the narration or are short enough to read in the shot's reading time.

pacing.question: Does the pacing report flag a shot as rushed, slack, unreadable, long or dense?
pacing.passes_when: No flag, or each flag accepted with a reason.

readability.question: Is every piece of text that must be read at least the legibility floor on the smallest planned display?
readability.passes_when: The legibility row has no size problem for must-read text, and the half-scale and quarter-scale sheets read.

readability.question: Is any text cut by the frame edge, a label, a callout, a transition or a camera move?
readability.passes_when: Every text element sits whole inside the safe area with nothing over it.

readability.question: Is text on screen for its reading time, 0.5 s plus 3 words per second?

captions.question: Do captions match what is said, word for word, including numbers as spoken?
captions.passes_when: The caption check lists no deviation without a decision.

captions.question: Do the sidecars pass the caption lint, agree with each other and follow the speech?
Do burned-in captions avoid the text, faces and controls the shot is about?
captions.passes_when: No caption covers what the line refers to.

claims.question: Does every number and factual claim, spoken or shown, match its evidence in the claim trace?
Are qualifiers kept wherever the evidence has them: made-up, one task, a local run, a date?
claims.passes_when: No claim reads stronger than its record.

claims.question: Do the words match the picture they sit on, such as a spoken label and the highlighted one?
claims.passes_when: No spoken term contradicts the text it highlights.

accessibility.question: Are captions provided for all speech?
accessibility.passes_when: Coverage of measured speech is at least 0.95.

accessibility.question: Does anything flash more than three times in one second, or flash a large bright area?
accessibility.passes_when: No black or flat-frame flash outside the plan, and no flash pattern on the strips.

accessibility.question: Does text meet 4.5 to 1 contrast, or 3 to 1 when large, and is nothing carried by color alone?
Is important visual information also spoken, or described?
accessibility.passes_when: A listener without the picture loses nothing that matters.

labels.question: Is every AI-generated voice, image or clip labeled where it appears, readably?
labels.passes_when: The label passes the legibility floor and is on screen whenever the voice or image is.

labels.question: Are made-up data, scripted stand-ins and illustrations labeled as such on screen?
labels.passes_when: Each appears with its label in the same shot.

labels.question: Does any capture show private data, a credential, a notification or a person who did not agree?

call_to_action.question: Does the ending give exactly one next step a viewer can act on?
call_to_action.passes_when: One step, named once in words and once on screen.

call_to_action.question: Does the end card hold long enough after the last word to read the address?
call_to_action.passes_when: The card's text stays for its reading time after the last word, or at least 2 s.

call_to_action.question: Is the address short enough to type or easy to find?
call_to_action.passes_when: A viewer can find it again from memory.

technical.question: Do the eight post-encode checks and the extended QA checks pass for these exact bytes, or is every failure explained?
technical.passes_when: Both reports name this file's digest and every failure has a decision.

technical.question: Has a person listened on headphones and on a phone speaker?
technical.passes_when: The listening record exists for these bytes.

answered_by.measured: A row of the video QA or video and motion checks gives the answer.
answered_by.panel: The reviewer answers from panels and full-size frames.
answered_by.judgment: The reviewer's judgment, written with its reason.

rules: Answer every question; a question that does not apply says why.

The rubric judges the video's own pixels and sound. The page and player around it, with the captions track loading, named controls, audio description and sound that starts on its own, belong to the accessibility audit pack's check-media; a single frame with known layout to the screenshot design review pack.
Score each area 1 to 5 from the anchors. A score never offsets a blocker.
A failed question becomes a finding at the severity it names, unless the evidence shows a lower one; say why.
Questions about real viewers belong to the video audience acceptance pack; this rubric judges the cut, not an audience.

nouns.title: Severity guide for video findings
nouns.category_reason: Fixed levels with their meanings and responses, so different reviewers rate the same problem the same way.

blocker.means: A wrong or untraced number or claim, a missing or unreadable AI or made-up-data label, private data on screen, a flash hazard, missing captions, or a broken file.
blocker.respond: Fix before any release. Never accepted with a reason.
blocker.findings_to_fixes: P1, or P0 when the cut is already published

major.means: Something most viewers will notice that weakens the point: must-read text too small or covered, a hook with nothing happening, text ghosted by a dissolve, captions out of sync, an ending that cannot be acted on.
major.respond: Fix before release, or a person accepts it in writing.

minor.means: Noticeable on a careful watch: a word clipped at an edge for a moment, a small overlap, a dip in pace, a spoken word that differs from the label it highlights.
minor.respond: Fix when nearby, or batch similar ones.

note.means: A taste call, an idea or a measurement worth keeping.

rules: Rate the effect on viewers and on trust, not the effort to fix.
Never lower a severity to make a cut look ready; a workaround is named when it lowers one.
Group findings that share a cause; fix the cause, not each frame.

nouns.title: Method: panels first, claims next, then the rubric
nouns.category_reason: A short ordered method every review follows, with the reason for each step.

steps: Hash the file and confirm every report and panel names the same digest.

Panels before opinions: a contact sheet at one frame per second, a hook strip of the first 3 s at four frames per second, an ending strip of the last 3 s and the first second, a strip at full frame rate from 0.5 s before to 0.5 s after each transition, and full-size frames at every text change.

Display-scale sheets: key frames at half size, about a phone held sideways for a 16:9 cut, and at a quarter, about a phone held upright. Text you cannot read there, a viewer on that screen cannot read either. They are a video's counterpart of the screenshot design review pack's capture matrix.

Contact sheets make dense text look worse than it is and full frames make small text look better than it will be on a phone; judge size on full frames and display-scale sheets, never on contact sheets.
Trace every claim before judging the story.
Answer the rubric with the QA rows in hand. Measure margins, timings and sizes instead of estimating them when a doubt matters.
Write each finding with its time range, area, severity, what was seen, how it was seen, its cause and the verb that would fix it.
End with the top fixes in priority order, the scores, what the review could not do, and a decision.
A second reviewer, ideally a different model or a person, answers the same rubric on the same panels; where they disagree, look again and record who was right.
A person listens once on headphones and once on a phone speaker. A worker reports that it could not listen.

verbs.summary: Watch the new file against every finding of the earlier review, mark each fixed, not fixed, regressed or no longer applicable with evidence from the new bytes, record new findings, and decide again without publishing.
verbs.outcome: A re-review of the new file.

slots.name: encoded_output
slots.description: Pin of the encoded file's media noun.

slots.name: previous_review
slots.description: Pin of the earlier review.

slots.name: panel_set
slots.description: Pin of the panels made from the new file.

steps: Confirm the new file's digest differs from the earlier review's and the panels name the new one.
Check every earlier finding at its time in the new file, with side-by-side frames where it helps.
Record anything newly broken as a new finding; decide again.

acceptance.check: The output validates against template.re-review's schema.
Every finding id of the earlier review has exactly one result.
A ready decision has open_blockers of 0.
